patient.name: Marcus Achterberg
patient.setting: Sexual health clinic, then the hepatology day unit
patient.complaint: Two weeks of tiredness, aching joints and an itchy rash, now with yellow eyes
background: Has sex with men; condomless sex with a new partner about 3 months ago
Drinks socially; no IV drug use

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' from the exposure (travel, sex, needles, pork, pregnancy) or from a serology block, where you must read HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM/IgG and HBeAg correctly.

points: Marcus, 31, has felt **wiped out** for two weeks.
His knees and wrists ache; he had an itchy **urticarial rash**.
Now his eyes are yellow and his urine is dark.
Condomless sex with a new partner **about 3 months ago**.

steps.lead: Marcus has a **hepatocellular** picture: his ALT is in the thousands with ALP only a little raised. That is the viral hepatitis pattern.

visual.title: Where Marcus is tender
visual.caption: A tender, smooth, enlarged liver: the inflamed capsule is stretched.

steps.lead: Sexual exposure in an MSM, unvaccinated: **hepatitis B** is top. Travel or shellfish would suggest A; pork or dirty water, E; IV drugs, C.

steps.q: Marcus's exposure was 3 months ago. Which virus fits best?
steps.r: Sexual spread, an incubation **over 2 months** and a prodrome of **urticaria and arthralgia** all point to hepatitis B.

steps.lead: His **urticaria and arthralgia** prodrome is classic acute hepatitis B; the serology will separate acute from chronic.

steps.title: The five hepatitis viruses at a glance
head: Virus
Spread
Chronic?
Vaccine?

steps.lead: If Marcus were a woman in her **third trimester** with jaundice after travel, think **hepatitis E**: high risk of fulminant liver failure.
If Marcus's hepatitis B becomes **chronic**, he risks cirrhosis and **hepatocellular carcinoma**; PAN is a rare vasculitic link.

steps.text: Do not assume a sexually acquired hepatitis is always B. **Hepatitis A** also spreads between MSM by oral-anal contact, so the serology decides.

investigation.exam: Expect a serology block and 'Which is the most likely interpretation?', or 'Which test confirms active hepatitis C?' (HCV RNA PCR) and 'Which marker shows high infectivity?' (HBeAg).

steps.title: Marcus's LFTs
steps.text: ALT-dominant hepatitis; normal INR and albumin mean synthetic function is holding.

visual.title: Marcus's ALT
visual.label: Marcus 1850
visual.caption: ALT in the thousands with modest ALP: acute hepatocellular injury.

steps.title: Viral hepatitis screen
steps.text: **Acute hepatitis B**, highly infectious (HBeAg and high HBV DNA).

steps.lead: Marcus's screen combines serology and PCR: **HBsAg plus anti-HBc IgM** is acute B; HBeAg means high infectivity. HDV is only tested because HBV is positive.

steps.q: Which result would show Marcus had cleared an old infection rather than having a new one?
steps.r: **Anti-HBc IgG** with negative HBsAg is past infection. IgM is acute; HBsAg is current infection.

visual.title: Hepatitis B markers over time in acute infection
visual.caption: HBsAg clears and anti-HBs appears if Marcus recovers. HBsAg still positive after 6 months = chronic.

steps.lead: Marcus's **INR** is 1.2 and albumin 38: no synthetic failure. In hepatitis C, **SVR** (undetectable RNA 12 weeks after therapy) means cure.

steps.text: **HBsAg** = infected now. **Anti-HBs** = immune (vaccine or recovery). **Anti-HBc** = has met the virus (IgM recent, IgG old). Vaccinated people have anti-HBs but **no anti-HBc**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' for a baby of an HBsAg/HBeAg-positive mother (vaccine plus HBIG within 24 h), chronic hepatitis B (tenofovir) or chronic hepatitis C (DAAs).

steps.q: Marcus has acute hepatitis B with a normal INR. What does he need now?
steps.r: Most adult acute hepatitis B clears on its own. **Supportive care**, LFT and INR monitoring, and recheck HBsAg at 6 months.

steps.lead: Marcus gets rest, fluids and **no alcohol**. If he were still HBsAg-positive with active disease after 6 months, he would start **tenofovir**.
If this were acute hepatitis C, the plan would also be monitoring; **PEGylated interferon plus ribavirin** is the historic option.
Marcus's partners need **contact screening**, vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis; hepatitis B vaccine also protects against hepatitis D.

steps.title: Hepatitis B post-exposure (sexual contact of Marcus)
nodes: Check contact's HBV status and vaccination history
Unvaccinated: HBIG plus accelerated hepatitis B vaccine course
Vaccinated responder: booster only if needed
steps.caption: Given ideally within 48 hours, up to 7 days after a sexual exposure.

visual.title: Months HBsAg-positive
visual.label: Marcus now
visual.caption: Recheck HBsAg at 6 months. Still positive = chronic, needs specialist review.

steps.lead: If a pregnant woman were Marcus's contact and HBsAg/HBeAg-positive, her baby needs **vaccine plus HBIG within 12–24 hours** of birth, then the full course.
Marcus's care follows **NICE** hepatitis B/C guidance and **BVHG** advice: test, notify, trace contacts and vaccinate.

steps.text: Chronic hepatitis C is **curable** with direct-acting antivirals. Do not pick interferon as first-line: it is historical.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why hepatitis D needs B (HBsAg envelope), why B becomes chronic (DNA integration), why liver damage in B is immune-mediated, and how DAAs work.

steps.lead: Marcus's virus is a partially double-stranded **DNA** virus; his jaundice is caused by his own **cytotoxic T-cells** killing infected hepatocytes.

steps.title: Why hepatitis B can become chronic and cause cancer
nodes: Cytotoxic T-cells attack infected cells: chronic inflammation

steps.lead: If Marcus became a chronic carrier, both **inflammation-driven cirrhosis** and **viral integration** would raise his cancer risk.
Hepatitis A and E are **non-enveloped RNA** viruses spread faeco-orally, causing self-limiting disease without chronic carriage.

steps.q: Why can hepatitis D only infect someone who already has hepatitis B?
o: It needs HBsAg for its envelope
steps.r: HDV is a **defective RNA virus** that borrows **HBsAg** to build its coat.

steps.lead: So vaccinating Marcus's partners against B also protects them from **hepatitis D**, which would otherwise accelerate damage.
Hepatitis C mutates fast and escapes immunity, so it often becomes chronic; **DAAs** hit NS3/4A, NS5A and NS5B to cure it.

mcq.q: Which hepatitis virus is particularly dangerous in the third trimester of pregnancy?
mcq.r: **Hepatitis E** carries a high risk of fulminant liver failure in late pregnancy.

mcq.q: Which vasculitis is associated with chronic hepatitis B?
mcq.r: **PAN**: hypertension, renal impairment, mononeuritis multiplex, livedo reticularis.

mcq.q: Which serological marker confirms acute hepatitis A?
Which hepatitis B marker indicates high infectivity?
What defines a sustained virological response in hepatitis C?
o: Undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after therapy

mcq.q: What is the first-line treatment class for chronic hepatitis C?
What is first-line treatment for active chronic hepatitis B?
For which hepatitis viruses is a vaccine available in the UK?
mcq.r: Vaccines exist for **A and B**; none for C, D or E.

mcq.q: Why can hepatitis D not exist without hepatitis B?
o: It needs HBsAg for its envelope
mcq.r: HDV is defective and uses **HBsAg** for its envelope.

technique.stem: A 34 year old man has 10 days of fatigue, arthralgia and an urticarial rash, followed by jaundice. He had condomless sex with a new partner 3 months ago. He has never been vaccinated. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis from a serology block: read each marker in turn.

clues: condomless sex with a new partner 3 months ago
steps.x: Prodrome of urticaria/arthralgia; sexual exposure; incubation over 2 months. Labs: HBsAg positive, **anti-HBc IgM** positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM = **acute hepatitis B**.

elim: Chronic B needs HBsAg for over 6 months, with anti-HBc IgG not IgM.
Vaccine immunity gives anti-HBs only, with HBsAg negative.
Anti-HCV is negative.
Past infection is HBsAg negative with anti-HBc IgG.

steps.x: **A. Acute hepatitis B.** Rule: IgM = acute; IgG = old; HBsAg = infected now.

technique.stem: A 26 year old woman has acute hepatitis A after a trip to Morocco. She is jaundiced and nauseated but alert. Her ALT is 2400 IU/L (10–50). The team wants to know whether her liver's synthetic function is failing.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: It asks about **synthetic function**, i.e. severity, not the cause.
Diagnosis known; ALT shows injury, not function.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **INR** is the best marker of synthetic function and severity.

elim: ALP reflects the biliary tree.
IgG shows past infection or immunity; IgM is the acute marker, and neither measures severity.
GGT is a cholestatic and alcohol marker.
Biopsy is not needed in acute viral hepatitis.

steps.x: **D. INR.** Rule: injury = ALT; function = INR and albumin.

technique.stem: A 28 year old nurse who has never been vaccinated against hepatitis B has a needlestick injury from a patient known to be HBsAg-positive. She washed the wound immediately. It is 2 hours since the injury.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin and accelerated vaccine course
Single dose of hepatitis B vaccine only

steps.x: Post-exposure management of hepatitis B.
Unvaccinated person, high-risk source, early presentation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatitis B **post-exposure prophylaxis**: HBIG plus an accelerated vaccine course.

elim: Tenofovir alone is HIV-style PEP; HBV PEP is HBIG plus vaccine.
Waiting misses the window for prophylaxis.
One vaccine dose gives no protection in time; she needs HBIG and a full course.
DAAs treat hepatitis C.

steps.x: **A. HBIG and accelerated vaccine.**

technique.stem: A 40 year old man with chronic hepatitis B is admitted with a sudden rise in ALT and jaundice. He injects drugs. Serology shows HBsAg positive and a new positive antibody to a second hepatitis virus that cannot replicate on its own.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason this second virus depends on hepatitis B?
o: It requires HBeAg to enter hepatocytes
It requires HBsAg to form its envelope
It requires immune suppression by HBV

steps.x: A mechanism question about hepatitis D.
HBV carrier with acute worsening after IV drug exposure: **hepatitis D superinfection**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HDV is a defective RNA virus that needs **HBsAg** for its envelope.

elim: HDV is an RNA virus and does not integrate into HBV DNA.
HBeAg is a marker of infectivity, not an entry protein for HDV.
HDV uses host RNA polymerase, not HBV reverse transcriptase.
HBV does not cause the immune suppression HDV would need.

steps.x: **C. HBsAg for its envelope.**

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman has 5 days of nausea, anorexia and jaundice. She returned from backpacking in Nepal 4 weeks ago, where she ate street food and drank tap water. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. She has tender hepatomegaly.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Jaundice with an ALT-dominant hepatitis 2 to 6 weeks after faeco-oral exposure abroad is acute hepatitis A.

steps.x: Diagnosis: traveller with jaundice. Look at timing and the LFT pattern.

clues: returned from backpacking in Nepal 4 weeks ago
street food and drank tap water
steps.x: Faeco-oral exposure, **4 weeks** incubation (2–6), afebrile, hepatomegaly; ALT-dominant LFTs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute hepatitis A**.

elim: Amoebic abscess gives a high swinging fever and a focal RUQ mass.
Gilbert's has normal ALT.
Malaria causes high fever, often low platelets, within weeks of travel.
Typhoid causes fever, bradycardia and abdominal pain, not ALT in the thousands.

steps.x: **A. Acute hepatitis A.**

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman at 32 weeks of pregnancy has a flu-like illness then jaundice, 5 weeks after returning from Bangladesh where she drank untreated water. Her BP is 118/72 mmHg and pulse rate 104 bpm. She is now drowsy. Her INR is 2.4 and platelets are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Waterborne exposure in South Asia then fulminant hepatitis in the third trimester is classic hepatitis E, which is particularly severe in late pregnancy.

steps.x: Diagnosis: pregnant traveller with a severe hepatitis.
Waterborne faeco-oral exposure; flu-like prodrome; **3rd trimester**; fulminant failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hepatitis E**.

elim: AFLP has no infective exposure and usually presents with pain then jaundice and hypoglycaemia.
HELLP needs hypertension and low platelets.
Hepatitis A rarely causes fulminant failure in pregnancy.
Obstetric cholestasis gives itch and raised bile acids, not liver failure.

steps.x: **D. Hepatitis E.** Severe in the third trimester; there is no UK vaccine.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man who moved from Nigeria 10 years ago has routine bloods for a new job. He feels well. Testing 8 months ago showed the same serology pattern.
practice.q: Which is the most likely interpretation?
practice.e: HBsAg positive for more than 6 months with anti-HBc IgG is chronic hepatitis B, often asymptomatic.

steps.x: Serology interpretation: HBsAg, then anti-HBc type, then time.
Endemic area, well, HBsAg positive for **over 6 months**, anti-HBc IgG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic hepatitis B**.

elim: Acute B has anti-HBc IgM.
Vaccination gives anti-HBs only, HBsAg negative.
Past infection is HBsAg negative and anti-HBs positive.
He is HBsAg positive, so infected.

steps.x: **B. Chronic hepatitis B.**

practice.stem: A 50 year old man has months of fatigue and a vague discomfort under his right ribs. He injected heroin for 3 years in his twenties. He drinks 6 units of alcohol a week. His BP is 128/80 mmHg and pulse rate 76 bpm. His ALT is 118 IU/L (10–50), AST 96 IU/L (10–40) and ALP 92 IU/L (25–115).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A distant history of injecting with fatigue, mild RUQ discomfort and disproportionately raised transaminases is chronic hepatitis C.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a silent chronic hepatitis.
Past **IV drug use**; subtle chronic symptoms; mild hepatitic LFTs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic hepatitis C**.

elim: 6 units a week is low, and AST is below ALT.
AIH favours young women with other autoimmunity.
Hepatitis A is acute and never chronic.
Hepatitis E is acute and self-limiting.

steps.x: **C. Chronic hepatitis C.**

practice.stem: A 52 year old man with chronic hepatitis B has new hypertension, weight loss and a right foot drop. His BP is 168/98 mmHg and pulse rate 90 bpm. He has a net-like purple rash on his legs. His creatinine is 168 μmol/L (60–110).
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication of his hepatitis?
practice.e: Hypertension, renal impairment, mononeuritis multiplex and livedo reticularis in chronic hepatitis B is polyarteritis nodosa.

steps.x: A complication question: match the systemic features.
Hypertension, mononeuritis multiplex (foot drop), **livedo reticularis**, renal impairment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Polyarteritis nodosa**, the vasculitis linked with hepatitis B.

elim: Cryoglobulinaemia is classically hepatitis C, with purpura and arthralgia.
HCC gives weight loss and a liver mass, not foot drop and livedo.
Hepatorenal syndrome occurs in decompensated cirrhosis with low BP, not hypertension.
IgA nephropathy gives haematuria after infection, not mononeuritis.

steps.x: **E. Polyarteritis nodosa.**

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman with known chronic hepatitis B, previously stable, has 2 weeks of worsening jaundice and confusion. She has recently started injecting drugs again. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 102/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
practice.e: A rapid, severe deterioration in a known HBV carrier after renewed injecting fits hepatitis D superinfection, which needs HBV and accelerates damage.

steps.x: Cause of sudden worsening in chronic hepatitis B.
HBV carrier + blood-borne exposure + rapid severe decline.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hepatitis D superinfection**.

elim: Hepatitis A is faeco-oral, not linked to injecting.
Hepatitis C is usually silent acutely and anti-HCV is negative.
Hepatitis E is faeco-oral, not blood-borne.
HCC is slow and would show a mass.

steps.x: **C. Hepatitis D superinfection.**

practice.stem: A 44 year old man who injected drugs in the past is found to be anti-HCV positive on screening. He feels well. His ALT is 86 IU/L (10–50).
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm active infection?
practice.e: Anti-HCV shows exposure but stays positive after clearance; HCV RNA PCR confirms active infection.

steps.x: 'Confirm active infection' in hepatitis C.
Antibody alone cannot tell active from cleared infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HCV RNA PCR**.

elim: There is no routine anti-HCV IgM test.
Biopsy stages damage but is not how infection is confirmed.
Ultrasound looks for cirrhosis or HCC, not active virus.
Antibody stays positive even after clearance.

steps.x: **B. HCV RNA PCR.**

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman at her 10 week booking visit is found to be HBsAg positive. She is well. Her BP is 112/70 mmHg and pulse rate 78 bpm. The midwife wants to know the risk of transmission to the baby.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: HBeAg (with HBV DNA) marks high infectivity; HBeAg-positive mothers have about a 90% risk of vertical transmission.

steps.x: Investigation to judge infectivity in hepatitis B.

clues: risk of transmission to the baby
steps.x: Already infected; the question is **how infectious**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HBeAg** (plus HBV DNA).

elim: Anti-HBc IgM says acute vs chronic, not infectivity.
Anti-HBs shows immunity, which she lacks.
INR is liver function, not infectivity.
Ultrasound checks the liver, not transmission risk.

steps.x: **C. HBeAg.**

practice.stem: A baby is born at term to a mother who is HBsAg positive and HBeAg positive. The baby is well, with a heart rate of 140 bpm. The mother asks what the baby needs.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 24 hours of birth
Hepatitis B vaccine at 8 weeks with routine immunisations
Separate baby from mother and avoid breastfeeding
Test the baby for HBsAg at 12 months then decide
practice.e: Babies of HBsAg/HBeAg-positive mothers need hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG within 12 to 24 hours of birth, then the full vaccine course.

steps.x: Management of a baby at high risk of vertical transmission.
HBeAg-positive mother: about **90%** transmission risk without prophylaxis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Vaccine plus HBIG** at birth, then complete the course.

elim: Waiting 8 weeks misses the window; the birth dose is critical.
Antivirals are not given to the newborn.
Breastfeeding is not contraindicated once prophylaxis is given.
Testing later without prophylaxis leaves the baby to be infected.

steps.x: **A. Vaccine and HBIG within 24 hours.**

practice.stem: A 47 year old woman has chronic hepatitis C confirmed by a positive HCV RNA PCR. She has no cirrhosis on Fibroscan. Her BP is 126/82 mmHg and pulse rate 72 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Chronic hepatitis C is treated with direct-acting antivirals such as sofosbuvir with velpatasvir; cure is shown by SVR at 12 weeks.

steps.x: First-line treatment of chronic hepatitis C.
Active, chronic infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **DAAs** (e.g. sofosbuvir/velpatasvir).

elim: Transplant is for decompensated cirrhosis or HCC.
Monitoring is for acute C; chronic C should be cured.
Interferon is historical.
Tenofovir treats hepatitis B.

steps.x: **A. Direct-acting antivirals.**

practice.stem: A 39 year old man has had HBsAg-positive chronic hepatitis B for 3 years. His ALT is persistently raised and HBV DNA is high. His BP is 130/84 mmHg and pulse rate 74 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
practice.e: Active chronic hepatitis B (raised ALT and high HBV DNA) is treated with tenofovir or entecavir, monitoring LFTs and HBV DNA.

steps.x: Treatment of active chronic hepatitis B.
Chronic, **active** disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Tenofovir** (or entecavir).

elim: Ribavirin is a hepatitis C drug; lamivudine is no longer first-line.
Steroids can flare HBV.
Sofosbuvir is a hepatitis C DAA.
Active chronic disease needs antiviral treatment.

steps.x: **E. Tenofovir.**

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has acute hepatitis B. His ALT is 2200 IU/L (10–50). His doctor explains that the virus itself does little direct damage to liver cells.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hepatocyte injury?
o: Cytotoxic T-cell attack on infected hepatocytes
practice.e: Liver damage in hepatitis B is largely immune-mediated by cytotoxic T-cells attacking infected hepatocytes, not directly cytopathic.

steps.x: A mechanism question: what kills the hepatocytes in HBV.
The stem tells you it is **not** cytopathic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cytotoxic T-cells** attack infected cells.

elim: Antibodies help clear virus but are not the main cause of injury.
The stem excludes direct cytopathic damage.
That is Budd-Chiari.
That is paracetamol (NAPQI).

steps.x: **B. Cytotoxic T-cell attack.**

prompts.q: How is each hepatitis virus (A to E) spread, and who is at risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the exposure in the stem names the virus.

points.p: A: faeco-oral, shellfish, unclean water, travel
B: blood, sex, perinatal (IVDU, MSM, sex workers)

prompts.q: What are the typical presentations of hepatitis A and B?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: incubation period and prodrome.

points.p: A: 2–6 week incubation, hepatomegaly, self-limiting, never chronic
Chronic B: HBsAg positive over 6 months, often asymptomatic

prompts.q: Which hepatitis is dangerous in pregnancy, and what other features does hepatitis E have?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: third trimester and fulminant failure.

points.p: Hepatitis E in the third trimester
points.why: High risk of fulminant acute liver failure.

points.p: Flu-like illness, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, sometimes diarrhoea

prompts.q: What are the complications of chronic hepatitis B and C?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: cancer, cirrhosis, vasculitis, vertical spread.

points.why: HBV can cause HCC even without cirrhosis.

points.p: Vertical transmission 90% if mother HBeAg positive
Hepatitis D accelerates hepatitis B damage

prompts.q: What LFT pattern does viral hepatitis give, and how does it differ from obstruction?

points.why: Often in the thousands in acute disease.

points.p: Only mildly raised ALP: hepatocellular pattern

prompts.q: Name the serology for each hepatitis virus.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one marker per virus, plus the HBV panel.

points.why: IgG means past infection or vaccine.

points.p: B: HBsAg current, anti-HBc IgM acute, IgG past/chronic
C: anti-HCV, confirmed by HCV RNA PCR
D: anti-HDV only if HBV positive; E: anti-HEV IgM

prompts.q: How do you assess severity and treatment response?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: INR for function, SVR for hepatitis C cure.

points.why: INR is the key synthetic marker.

points.p: Hepatitis C: SVR = undetectable RNA 12 weeks after therapy

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: A supportive, chronic B tenofovir, chronic C DAAs.

points.why: Also D and E: rest, hydration, no alcohol.
If active disease; monitor HBV DNA.

prompts.q: How are hepatitis B infections prevented, including in newborns?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: vaccine, PEP, contacts, the baby.

points.p: Vaccines for A and B only
points.why: None for C, D or E; B vaccine prevents D too.

points.p: Baby of HBsAg/HBeAg+ mother: vaccine plus HBIG within 12–24 hours

prompts.q: Why do hepatitis B and C become chronic, but A and E do not?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: virus structure decides chronicity.

points.p: A and E: non-enveloped RNA viruses, self-limiting
points.why: E can be chronic if immunosuppressed.

points.p: B: DNA virus that integrates into hepatocyte DNA
B damage is immune-mediated by cytotoxic T-cells
C: RNA virus with high mutation rate escapes immunity

prompts.q: Why does hepatitis D need hepatitis B?

glossary.HAV: Hepatitis A virus, a faeco-orally spread RNA virus causing acute hepatitis only.
glossary.HBV: Hepatitis B virus, a blood-borne DNA virus that can cause chronic infection.
glossary.HCV: Hepatitis C virus, a blood-borne RNA virus that is often chronic and silent.
glossary.HDV: Hepatitis D (delta) virus, a defective virus that needs hepatitis B to survive.
glossary.HEV: Hepatitis E virus, a faeco-orally spread virus that is dangerous in late pregnancy.
glossary.HBsAg: Hepatitis B surface antigen; positive means current infection.
glossary.anti-HBs: Antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen; means immunity from vaccine or recovery.
glossary.anti-HBc: Antibody to hepatitis B core antigen; shows natural infection (IgM recent, IgG past or chronic).
glossary.HBeAg: Hepatitis B e antigen; marks active replication and high infectivity.
glossary.HBV DNA: Viral load of hepatitis B in the blood.
glossary.HBIG: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin: ready-made antibodies given for immediate protection after exposure.
glossary.anti-HCV: Antibody to hepatitis C; shows exposure but not whether infection is still active.
glossary.PCR: Polymerase chain reaction, a test that detects viral genetic material.
glossary.SVR: Sustained virological response: undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after treatment, meaning cure.
glossary.DAA: Direct-acting antiviral; drugs that block hepatitis C proteins and cure most patients.
glossary.sofosbuvir: A hepatitis C DAA that blocks the NS5B polymerase.
glossary.velpatasvir: A hepatitis C DAA that blocks NS5A.
glossary.ledipasvir: A hepatitis C DAA that blocks NS5A.
glossary.ribavirin: An antiviral sometimes added to hepatitis C treatment.
glossary.tenofovir: A nucleotide analogue antiviral, first-line for chronic hepatitis B.
glossary.entecavir: A nucleoside analogue antiviral used for chronic hepatitis B.
glossary.PEGylated interferon: A long-acting injected interferon, the historic treatment for hepatitis B and C.
glossary.IgM: The first antibody made in an infection; marks acute or recent infection.
glossary.IgG: The later, long-lasting antibody; marks past or chronic infection.
glossary.faeco-oral: Spread by swallowing material contaminated with faeces.
glossary.vertical transmission: Spread of infection from mother to baby around birth.
glossary.MSM: Men who have sex with men.
glossary.PAN: Polyarteritis nodosa, a medium-vessel vasculitis linked with hepatitis B.
glossary.polyarteritis nodosa: Medium-vessel vasculitis causing hypertension, renal impairment, mononeuritis multiplex and livedo; linked to hepatitis B.
glossary.mononeuritis multiplex: Damage to two or more separate named nerves, e.g. causing foot drop.
glossary.livedo reticularis: A net-like purple mottling of the skin.
glossary.hepatocellular carcinoma: Primary liver cancer arising from hepatocytes.
glossary.fulminant: Sudden and severe, as in rapid-onset liver failure.
glossary.superinfection: A second infection on top of an existing one, e.g. HDV in a hepatitis B carrier.
glossary.post-exposure prophylaxis: Treatment given soon after exposure to prevent infection taking hold.
glossary.Fibroscan: An ultrasound-based test that measures liver stiffness to stage fibrosis.
glossary.INR: International normalised ratio; a clotting test that shows liver synthetic function.
glossary.ALT: Alanine aminotransferase, an enzyme released by damaged hepatocytes.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase, raised mainly in biliary obstruction.
glossary.cytotoxic T-cells: Immune cells that kill virus-infected cells; they cause most of the liver damage in hepatitis B.
glossary.hepatocellular: Relating to liver cells; a hepatocellular LFT pattern means ALT-dominant injury.
